hero.title: National Income — Measuring an Entire Economy
hero.hook: How do economists measure the total output of an economy with 1.4 billion people, millions of firms, and thousands of products? They use National Income — a set of concepts and methods that capture the value of everything produced in a country in a year. GDP, GNP, NNP — these aren't just abbreviations, they're windows into how a nation is doing.

hook_section.scenario: India produces rice, software, cars, movies, and medical services — all in the same year. How do you add rice and software? You can't add tons of grain to lines of code. The solution: measure everything in money (market value). The total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year — that's GDP. And how you measure it, adjust it, and interpret it makes all the difference in economics.
hook_section.bridge: National Income accounting is Chapter 2 of Class 12 Macro Economics. It's tested every year with definitional questions and numerical problems. The key is knowing the relationships between GDP, GNP, NNP, NI, PI, and DPI — and when to use which method (income, output, expenditure) to calculate them.
hook_section.punchline: Three methods, same answer: Output Method = Income Method = Expenditure Method. They all measure the same circular flow from different angles.

concept_section.analogy: The economy is a circular flow — firms produce goods, pay wages to workers, workers buy goods from firms. National income can be measured at any point in this circle: at production (output method), at payment (income method), or at spending (expenditure method). Like measuring water in a pipe — you can measure flow at the input, the pump, or the output. Same water, different measurement points.
concept_section.principle: GDP at Market Price = C + I + G + (X−M) [Expenditure method]. GNP = GDP + NFIA. NNP = GNP − Depreciation. NNP at Factor Cost = NI = NNP at Market Price − Net Indirect Taxes. NFIA = Net Factor Income from Abroad.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each concept to master the relationships 👇

reveals.question: 📊 GDP vs GNP vs NNP?
reveals.answer: GDP: value of final goods/services produced within country's boundaries (by residents AND non-residents). GNP = GDP + NFIA (includes income earned abroad by nationals, excludes income earned in India by foreigners). NNP = GNP − Depreciation (Net National Product). NNP at Factor Cost = National Income.

reveals.question: 🔧 Three methods of measurement?
reveals.answer: Output/Product Method: sum of value added by each firm (avoids double counting). Income Method: sum of factor incomes (wages + rent + interest + profit). Expenditure Method: C + I + G + (X−M). All three give same GDP if measured correctly.

reveals.question: 💰 From NNP to DPI?
reveals.answer: NNP at Market Price → minus Net Indirect Taxes → National Income → minus Undistributed profits, Corporate taxes, Social security → plus Transfer payments → Personal Income → minus Direct personal taxes → Disposable Personal Income (DPI).

reveals.question: 🌍 Real vs Nominal GDP?
reveals.answer: Nominal GDP: at current prices (includes inflation). Real GDP: at constant base year prices (removes inflation effect). GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Real GDP better measures actual growth in output.

points: GDP: value of final goods/services within territorial boundaries in a year
GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − Depreciation; NNP at FC = National Income
Three methods: Output (value added), Income (factor incomes), Expenditure (C+I+G+NX) — all give same result
Double counting avoided: by counting only final goods OR by counting only value added
Real GDP: at constant prices; removes inflation; better measure of actual economic growth

exam_questions.question: Calculate NNP at Market Price from the following: GDP at Market Price = ₹500 crore, Depreciation = ₹20 crore, NFIA = ₹30 crore.
Explain the Income Method of calculating national income. What are the four factor incomes included?
What is the relationship between GDP and GNP?

quiz.q: NNP at Factor Cost is equal to:
quiz.exp: NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price − Net Indirect Taxes = National Income. Also, NNP = GNP − Depreciation. So NNP at FC = GNP − Depreciation − Net Indirect Taxes = National Income.

quiz.q: If GDP = ₹1000 cr, NFIA = ₹50 cr, Depreciation = ₹100 cr. NNP at MP =
quiz.exp: NNP at MP = GNP − Depreciation = (GDP + NFIA) − Depreciation = (1000 + 50) − 100 = ₹950 cr.

quiz.q: To avoid double counting in GDP, which method is used?
opts: Count final goods or value added
quiz.exp: Double counting is avoided by counting only FINAL goods (not intermediate ones) in the product method, or by counting only VALUE ADDED at each stage of production.

quiz.q: Real GDP differs from Nominal GDP because:
opts: It is measured at base year prices
quiz.exp: Real GDP uses constant base-year prices to eliminate the effect of inflation. Nominal GDP uses current prices. When prices rise, nominal GDP rises even if real output doesn't — real GDP shows true growth.

flipcards.back: GNP = GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad)
Net Factor Income from Abroad = Income earned by nationals abroad − Income earned by foreigners in India
NNP = GNP − Depreciation (Consumption of Fixed Capital)
NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price − Net Indirect Taxes

flipcards.front: What is the expenditure method formula?
flipcards.back: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); C=Consumption, I=Investment, G=Govt spending, X=Exports, M=Imports
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100; measures price level change
